rag-pipelines.title: Building Production RAG Pipelines
rag-pipelines.excerpt: From chunking strategies to observability — how to ship retrieval systems that survive real traffic.

sections.heading: The demo-to-production gap
paragraphs: A RAG that dazzles in a demo can collapse once it meets noisy documents, traffic spikes, or ambiguous questions. The difference rarely sits in the model alone — it sits in the pipeline.
In production, retrieval must stay stable, measurable, and revisable. Without those guardrails, you ship a brilliant experience… until the first business incident.

sections.heading: Chunking, embeddings, and ranking
paragraphs: Aggressive chunking breaks context; oversized chunks dilute signal. I prefer a hybrid approach: semantic chunks, controlled overlaps, and rich metadata (source, date, document type).
Then comes ranking. Simple vector top-k is not enough. Combining dense similarity, business filters, and light re-ranking improves relevance drastically without exploding latency.

sections.heading: Observability and the improvement loop
paragraphs: Without traces, you fly blind. I log queries, selected chunks, scores, and user feedback. Those signals feed continuous evals: perceived precision, hallucination rate, p95 latency.
The real deliverable is not a chatbot. It is a reliable retrieval system with clear improvement levers and an architecture ready to evolve.

data-engineering-path.title: My Path Into Data Engineering
data-engineering-path.excerpt: Lessons from moving from full-stack product work to pipelines, warehouses, and reliable data platforms.

sections.heading: Why this transition
paragraphs: After years shipping full-stack products and AI systems, one truth became obvious: without reliable data, intelligence stays fragile. Models, dashboards, and automations all depend on a sound foundation.
Moving into Data Engineering is not leaving product behind. It is stepping one layer deeper to build the infrastructure that makes product durable.

sections.heading: What I had to relearn
paragraphs: The craft changes: orchestration (Airflow), transformations (dbt), modeling, data contracts, quality, and lineage. You no longer code only for a UI — you code for flows, SLAs, and downstream teams.
Product rigor still helps. A readable, tested, documented pipeline behaves like a good React component: clear, predictable, maintainable.

sections.heading: What I build now
paragraphs: I connect both worlds: APIs and apps on one side, pipelines and warehouses on the other. The goal is simple — intelligent products backed by trustworthy data.
That trajectory guides my work today: fewer throwaway prototypes, more systems that hold over time.

nextjs-performance.title: Next.js Performance Patterns
nextjs-performance.excerpt: Practical patterns for faster navigations, smarter caching, and Lighthouse scores that hold in production.

sections.heading: Measure before you optimize
paragraphs: Performance starts with numbers: LCP, INP, CLS, JS weight, network waterfall. Without a baseline, you optimize by feel — and often miss the real bottleneck.
I set two or three budgets first (initial JS, hero images, time to interaction), then work by descending impact.

sections.heading: Patterns that scale
paragraphs: Streaming, lazy-loading heavy sections, responsive images, HTTP/CDN caching, and cutting unnecessary re-renders. On Vite/React as on Next, the principle stays the same: load less, earlier, and only what matters.
Design systems are part of the equation too. Too many animations, fonts, or decorative JS — and Lighthouse collapses. Visual restraint is a performance strategy.

sections.heading: Keeping performance over time
paragraphs: Good performance must be protected: CI budgets, RUM monitoring, dependency reviews. Otherwise every feature silently erodes it.
Ship fast, yes. But ship fast and stay fast — that is real frontend craft.
